causes.text: Verizon dominated the 2021 C-band spectrum auction, spending $45.45 billion on 3,500 licenses to secure high-capacity 5G spectrum, nearly double the amount spent by other bidders.

source_info.title: Verizon dominated the C Band auction, spending $45.45 billion for 3,511 licenses

effects.text: On 5 December 2023, AT&T announced plans to invest up to $14 billion over five years to deploy a commercial-scale Open RAN wireless network in collaboration with Ericsson, aiming to carry 70% of its traffic on open-enabled platforms by late 2026.

source_info.title: AT&T collaborates with Ericsson to accelerate Open RAN deployment

causal_reasoning_chain.description: Verizon's aggressive spending of $45.45 billion in the C-band auction provided it with a large swath of mid-band spectrum licenses, strengthening its 5G network advantage over rivals.
Faced with Verizon's spectrum edge, AT&T pursued a major infrastructure shift by partnering with Ericsson to deploy a commercial-scale Open RAN network, committing up to $14 billion over five years.
The move signals a strategic response to Verizon's spectrum dominance, positioning AT&T to increase capacity and flexibility while modernizing its network architecture, the stock price rose 3.36%.

rationale: Verizon's spectrum dominance created a competitive imperative for AT&T. To close the infrastructure gap and remain competitive in 5G deployment, AT&T opted to invest in Open RAN and partner with Ericsson, signaling strategic adaptation to rival moves.
counterfactual_analysis: If Verizon had not secured such a large swath of C-band spectrum, AT&T may have stayed on traditional proprietary network designs rather than incurring high capital expenditure to shift to Open RAN.

adversarial_confounders.text: Government initiatives promoting open networks and evolving industry standards
adversarial_confounders.impact: Regulatory policy and overarching trends toward virtualization may also drive Open RAN adoption regardless of Verizon's spectrum position.

details.commentary: Verizon's massive C-band spend raised the stakes in the race for 5G leadership, signaling a willingness to invest heavily to defend share. Faced with that escalation, AT&T's pivot to an Open RAN build with Ericsson was a strategic response to stay competitive on network quality and cost.

Verizon's spectrum move heightened expectations for faster 5G rollouts, prompting AT&T to commit capital and partnerships that will shape its network for years. As each operator reacts to the other's investments, the arms race in 5G infrastructure reinforces itself, tying future traffic and returns to large, sunk build-out decisions.
